title: Option & Result: Error Handling
summary: No null, no exceptions. Model absence with Option, failure with Result, propagate with ?, and give your errors names with custom enums.

quest.title: The Damaged Treasure Map
quest.story:
The last voyage of the Crab Fleet's first season ends in a storm. When the sea calms, the captain unrolls the treasure map and groans: salt water has smeared half the ink. Some lines still read `N 3` or `E 10`. Others say `E x`, `Q 5`, or nothing at all.

The old quartermaster's map reader treated every line as perfect. It called `.unwrap()` on everything, and the first smudge sank the whole program with a **panic**.

On this crew, **any line can be bad**, and a good program says *which* line and *why*, instead of crashing. Rust has no `null` and no exceptions. It has `Option` for "maybe nothing", `Result` for "maybe failed", and the `?` operator to pass failures upward without drowning in `match`.

Learn them, read the damaged map, and finish your first season as a full member of the Crab Fleet.

concepts.title: Option<T> instead of null
concepts.body:
Rust has no `null`. A value that might be missing has the type `Option<T>`:

```rust
enum Option<T> {
    Some(T),
    None,
}
```

The compiler will not let you use an `Option<u32>` as a `u32`. You have to say what happens in the `None` case, so "forgot to check for null" cannot happen.

```rust
let crew = ["Ann", "Bo"];
let third: Option<&&str> = crew.get(2); // None, not a crash
```

`Option<String>` and `Option<Box<T>>` take no extra space: `None` is stored as a null pointer internally, and you never see it.

concepts.title: Result<T, E> and pattern matching
Combinators: transform without matching
concepts.body:
Small `match`es often collapse into a method call:

- `opt.map(|x| x * 2)` transforms the `Some` value. `None` stays `None`.
- `opt.and_then(f)` chains a step that can itself fail (`f` returns an `Option`).
- `opt.ok_or(err)` / `opt.ok_or_else(|| err)` turns `Option` into `Result`.
- `res.ok()` turns `Result` into `Option` and throws the error away.
- `res.map_err(f)` changes the error type.
- `x.unwrap_or(default)`, `x.unwrap_or_default()` give a fallback value. These never panic.

```rust
let depth = "40".parse::<u32>().unwrap_or(0);       // 40
let depth = "deep".parse::<u32>().unwrap_or_default(); // 0
```

concepts.title: The ? operator
concepts.body:
`?` means: "if this is `Err` (or `None`), **return it from the current function right now**. Otherwise give me the value inside."

```rust
fn double(s: &str) -> Result<u32, ParseIntError> {
    let n: u32 = s.parse()?; // early return on Err
    Ok(n * 2)
}
```

Two rules the compiler enforces with **E0277**:

1. The function must itself return `Result` (or `Option` for `?` on an `Option`). Using `?` in a plain `fn main()` that returns `()` is an error. `fn main() -> Result<(), E>` is allowed.
2. The error must convert into the function's error type. `?` calls `From::from` on the error, so `ParseIntError` cannot silently become `String`. Use `.map_err(...)?` or implement `From`.

concepts.title: unwrap, expect and panics
concepts.body:
`.unwrap()` takes the value out of `Some`/`Ok` and **panics** on `None`/`Err`. `.expect("msg")` does the same with your message. A panic unwinds the thread, and from `main` that ends the program with exit code **101**.

Panicking is right when a failure means **a bug in your program**, not bad input: tests, examples, and invariants you have just checked. For anything that comes from outside (user input, files, the network, a damaged map), return a `Result` and let the caller decide. Library code should almost never `unwrap`.

concepts.title: Custom error enums with Display and From

visual.title: Option and Result in memory, and ? popping a frame

steps.note: Some(String) holds a normal String: pointer, length, capacity. The buffer "X" lives on the heap.
None allocates nothing. It is stored as a null pointer inside the same space, so Option<String> is no bigger than String.
parse("21") pushes a frame. s.parse() returns Ok(21), and ? unwraps it into n.
The happy path reaches the end: parse returns Ok(42), its frame is popped, and a holds the Result.
parse("x"): s.parse() returns Err(InvalidDigit). The ? sees the Err and does not bind n.
? returns early: the frame is popped right away, line 3 never runs, and b receives the Err.
End of main: map drops its String and frees the buffer. lost, a and b own nothing on the heap.

challenges.title: Unwrapping the lost island
challenges.story: The old quartermaster trusted every chart. One of these islands is not on any of them.
challenges.prompt: Read the program. What happens when you compile and run it?

choices.label: It prints `found at 7`, then panics at runtime (exit code 101)
Compile error E0308: `find_island` might return `None`, which is not a `u32`
It prints only `found at 7`: the second line is skipped because `b` is `None`

hints: What does `find_island("Atlantis")` return?
`unwrap()` on `Some(v)` gives `v`. What can it possibly give on `None`?
The type checker is happy: `unwrap()` returns `u32`. The problem only shows up when the program runs and meets a `None`.

challenges.title: Reading smudged ink
challenges.story: The navigator does all her chart reading with combinators and never writes a `match`. Can you follow her?
hints: `map` and `and_then` on `None` do nothing and return `None`. They never panic.
`and_then` keeps the result of the closure. Here the closure returns `None` unless the number is bigger than 5.
`ok_or(e)` turns `Some(v)` into `Ok(v)` and `None` into `Err(e)`.

challenges.title: A question mark in main
challenges.story: A deckhand learned about `?` this morning and is now putting it everywhere.
challenges.prompt: Read the program. What happens when you compile and run it?

choices.label: Compile error E0277: `?` can only be used in a function that returns `Result` or `Option`
Compile error E0308: `parse` returns a `Result`, not a `u32`
It compiles, but panics because `main` cannot return an error

hints: `?` may *return* from the current function. Which function is that, and what does it return?
`fn main()` with no return type returns `()`. Can `()` hold an `Err`?
rustc rejects this at compile time with E0277. The fix is `fn main() -> Result<(), std::num::ParseIntError>` plus `Ok(())` at the end, or handling the error with `match`.

challenges.title: Errors that don't fit
challenges.story: The diver's depth reader returns `String` errors, but the parser speaks `ParseIntError`. *Rustc* the parrot refuses to translate.
challenges.prompt:
This program does not compile: the `?` in `parse_depth` cannot convert a `ParseIntError` into the function's `String` error type (E0277).

Fix it so it prints exactly:

```text
dive to 40
dive to 7
cannot dive: 200 fathoms is too deep
cannot dive: bad depth "deep": invalid digit found in string
```

A bad number gives the error `bad depth "<input>": <parse error>`, where `<input>` is the original argument printed with `{:?}` and `<parse error>` is the `ParseIntError`'s `Display` text.

Rules: keep the signature `fn parse_depth(s: &str) -> Result<u32, String>` and keep using `?` for the parse. No `.unwrap()` or `.expect(`. `main` stays as it is.
hints: Read the E0277 message: `?` couldn't convert the error to `String`. Which two error types are involved?
`?` only converts errors through `From`, and there is no `From<ParseIntError> for String`. You can change the error yourself before the `?`.
`Result::map_err` transforms the `Err` value: `.parse().map_err(|e| format!("bad depth {s:?}: {e}"))?`.

cases.name: good, padded, too deep and bad depths
cases.expected:
dive to 40
dive to 7
cannot dive: 200 fathoms is too deep
cannot dive: bad depth "deep": invalid digit found in string

require.message: Keep using ? to propagate the parse error.

forbid.message: No .unwrap(): a bad depth must become an Err, not a panic.
No .expect(): a bad depth must become an Err, not a panic.

challenges.title: Cargo manifest helpers
challenges.story: Half the cargo manifest is legible. The purser needs three small helpers that never crash, whatever the ink says.
challenges.prompt:
Fill in the three `todo!()`s. None of them may panic.

- `fn parse_entry(line: &str) -> Option<(&str, u32)>`: a line looks like `rum = 12`. Split at the first `=`, trim both sides, and parse the count as `u32`. Return `None` if there is no `=`, the trimmed name is empty, or the count doesn't parse.
- `fn count_of(entries: &[(&str, u32)], name: &str) -> Result<u32, String>`: the count of the first entry named `name`, or `Err` with exactly `no crate named <name>`.
- `fn count_or_zero(s: &str) -> u32`: the trimmed text parsed as `u32`, or `0` if it doesn't parse.

Good tools for this: `let ... else`, `.ok()?`, `.find(...)`, `.map(...)`, `.ok_or_else(...)` and `.unwrap_or_default()`. Hidden tests call the three functions directly.
hints: `str::split_once('=')` returns `Option<(&str, &str)>`. `"12".parse::<u32>()` returns a `Result`, and `.ok()` turns it into an `Option`.

In a function returning `Option`, `?` works on `Option` values too: `let count = text.parse().ok()?;`. For the split, `let Some((name, count)) = line.split_once('=') else { return None; };` keeps the code flat.
`count_of`: `entries.iter().find(|(n, _)| *n == name).map(|&(_, c)| c).ok_or_else(|| format!("no crate named {name}"))`. `count_or_zero`: `s.trim().parse().unwrap_or_default()`.

forbid.message: No .unwrap(): these helpers must never panic.
No .expect(): these helpers must never panic.

challenges.title: Name your errors
challenges.story: The purser is tired of errors that just say *something went wrong*. Every damaged line deserves a proper name.
challenges.prompt:
Write a custom error type and two functions that use it. Use exactly these names:

```rust
use std::fmt;
use std::num::ParseIntError;

#[derive(Debug)]
enum CargoError {
    Empty,
    MissingCount(String),
    BadCount(ParseIntError),
}
```

- `impl fmt::Display for CargoError` with these messages:
  - `Empty`: `empty line`
  - `MissingCount(line)`: `no count in "<line>"` (the line printed with `{:?}`)
  - `BadCount(e)`: `bad count: <e>`
- `impl From<ParseIntError> for CargoError`, producing `BadCount`.
- `fn parse_line(line: &str) -> Result<(String, u32), CargoError>`: a line looks like `rum: 12`. Trim the line. If it is empty, return `Empty`. If it has no `:`, return `MissingCount` with the trimmed line. Otherwise the name is the trimmed text before the first `:` and the count is the trimmed text after it, parsed as `u32` with `?`.
- `fn total(manifest: &str) -> Result<u32, CargoError>`: the sum of the counts of **every** line (`str::lines`), or the error of the first bad line.

Keep a `fn main()`. Hidden tests call `parse_line`, `total`, `CargoError::from` and `to_string()`. After they pass, the tutor judges how idiomatic your error handling is.
hints: Start with the enum and `Display`: `match self { CargoError::Empty => write!(f, "empty line"), ... }`.
`impl From<ParseIntError> for CargoError { fn from(e: ParseIntError) -> Self { ... } }` is what lets `count.trim().parse()?` compile inside `parse_line`.

`parse_line`: trim, check `is_empty()`, then `let Some((name, count)) = line.split_once(':') else { return Err(CargoError::MissingCount(line.to_string())); };`, then `let count: u32 = count.trim().parse()?;`. `total`: loop over `manifest.lines()`, `let (_, c) = parse_line(line)?;` and add.

require.message: Implement From<ParseIntError> for CargoError so ? can convert the parse error.
Propagate errors with ? instead of matching every Result by hand.

forbid.message: No .unwrap() in parse_line or total: return the error instead.
No .expect() in parse_line or total: return the error instead.

challenges.rubric: Idiomatic Rust error handling. Required: no unwrap/expect/panic! in parse_line or total (library code returns errors, it does not crash); the parse error reaches the caller through ? using the From<ParseIntError> impl, not via a hand-written match on the parse result or map_err to a different variant; total uses ? inside the loop (or an iterator collecting into Result, e.g. map(parse_line).map(|r| r.map(|(_, c)| c)).sum::<Result<u32, _>>()), not nested matches. Display uses write! with a match on self and produces the exact messages; it is not built by matching on Debug output. Errors carry meaningful data (the offending trimmed line, the original ParseIntError), never a bare String or a lossy conversion to text. Prefer let-else or if-let/split_once over manual find+slice index arithmetic. Deduct points for: cloning or allocating more than needed (to_string on the name is fine since the tuple owns a String), swallowing errors with ok()/unwrap_or, deeply nested match pyramids, or redundant checks. Readability matters more than cleverness.

challenges.title: Boss: The Damaged Treasure Map
challenges.story: The captain hands you the soaked map and the old quartermaster's reader. It works on a perfect map and sinks on the first smudge. Make it survive the storm, and the treasure is the fleet's.
challenges.prompt:
The program reads a treasure map from stdin and follows it. Each line is `DIR DISTANCE`: a direction `N`, `S`, `E` or `W`, then a distance (`u32`), separated by whitespace. Start at `(0, 0)`. `E` increases x, `W` decreases x, `N` increases y and `S` decreases y. Lines are trimmed and blank lines are skipped.

Today it **panics** on any damaged line. Rewrite it so it never panics. For a good map such as

```text
N 3
E 10

S 1
W 4
```

it prints exactly:

```text
4 steps followed
treasure at (6, 2)
```

At the **first** damaged line it prints exactly one line, nothing else, and still exits normally:

```text
map damaged at line <n>: <error>
```

`<n>` is the 1-based line number in the input, with blank lines counted. `<error>` is one of these, checked in this order:

- the line does not have exactly two whitespace-separated parts: `expected DIR DISTANCE, got "<line>"` (the trimmed line printed with `{:?}`)
- unknown direction: `unknown direction "<dir>"` (printed with `{:?}`)
- the distance doesn't parse as `u32`: `bad distance: <ParseIntError message>`

Rules:
- Define an error enum that implements `Display` and `From<ParseIntError>`, and parse the distance with `.parse()?` (or `.parse::<u32>()?`) so `?` does the conversion.
- No `.unwrap()`, `.expect(` or `panic!` anywhere. Reading stdin can fail too: `main` may return `std::io::Result<()>`.

Hidden cases include an empty map, unknown directions, negative and huge distances, and lines with too many or too few parts.
hints: Split the work: a function that parses **one** line into a step and returns `Result<_, MapError>`, and a loop that adds the steps up and remembers the line number.

Your enum needs three variants: wrong shape (keep the line), unknown direction (keep the direction), bad distance (keep the `ParseIntError`). With `impl From<ParseIntError> for MapError`, `dist.parse::<u32>()?` converts automatically.
Collect `line.split_whitespace()` into a `Vec<&str>` and destructure with `let [dir, dist] = parts[..] else { return Err(...) };`. Check the direction with a `match` **before** parsing the distance.

In the loop, attach the line number with `parse_step(line).map_err(|e| (i + 1, e))?` inside a function returning `Result<(usize, i64, i64), (usize, MapError)>`. Make `main` return `io::Result<()>` so `read_to_string(&mut text)?` replaces the `unwrap()`.

cases.name: good map with a blank line
smudged distance
cases.expected: map damaged at line 2: bad distance: invalid digit found in string

cases.name: unknown direction after a blank line
cases.expected: map damaged at line 3: unknown direction "Q"

cases.name: missing distance
cases.expected: map damaged at line 2: expected DIR DISTANCE, got "E"

cases.name: too many parts
cases.expected: map damaged at line 1: expected DIR DISTANCE, got "N 3 4"

cases.name: negative distance and padding
cases.expected: map damaged at line 2: bad distance: invalid digit found in string

cases.name: huge distance
cases.expected: map damaged at line 1: bad distance: number too large to fit in target type

cases.name: first error wins, direction before distance
cases.expected: map damaged at line 1: unknown direction "Q"

require.message: Parse the distance with .parse()? so the From<ParseIntError> conversion does the work.
Implement From<ParseIntError> for your error enum.
Implement Display for your error enum.

forbid.message: No .unwrap(): a damaged map must produce an error message, not a panic.
No .expect(): a damaged map must produce an error message, not a panic.
No panic!: report the damaged line instead.

cards.front: How does Rust represent "maybe there is no value" without `null`?
cards.back: With `Option<T>`: `Some(value)` or `None`. The compiler won't let you use an `Option<T>` as a `T`, so you must handle `None`. `Option<String>` and `Option<Box<T>>` are no bigger than the pointer itself: `None` uses the null niche.

cards.front: What does `.unwrap()` do on `None` or `Err`, and when is that acceptable?
cards.back: It **panics**, and from `main` the program exits with code **101**. It's acceptable when failure would be a bug (tests, examples, invariants you just checked), not for input from outside. `.expect("why")` is the same, with a better message.

cards.front: `Some(4).and_then(|n| if n > 5 { Some(n) } else { None })` and `None::<u32>.ok_or("no map")` evaluate to?
cards.back: `None` and `Err("no map")`. `and_then` keeps whatever the closure returns. `ok_or(e)` maps `Some(v)` to `Ok(v)` and `None` to `Err(e)`. Neither ever panics.

cards.front: Why does `let n: u32 = "4".parse()?;` fail to compile inside `fn main()`?
cards.back: **E0277**: `?` may return early, so the enclosing function must return `Result` (or `Option`). Plain `main` returns `()`. Use `fn main() -> Result<(), ParseIntError>` and end with `Ok(())`, or handle the error with `match`.

cards.front: A function returns `Result<u32, String>` and does `s.parse::<u32>()?`. Why E0277, and what are two fixes?
cards.back: `?` converts the error with `From::from`, and there is no `From<ParseIntError> for String`. Fix 1: `.map_err(|e| format!("bad: {e}"))?`. Fix 2: use your own error type with `impl From<ParseIntError> for MyError`.

cards.front: What does `let Some((a, b)) = s.split_once('=') else { return None; };` do?
cards.back: **let-else**: if the pattern matches, `a` and `b` are bound for the rest of the function. Otherwise the `else` block runs, and it must diverge (`return`, `continue`, `break`, panic). It keeps code flat instead of nesting a `match`.

cards.front: What do you implement so `?` turns a `ParseIntError` into your `CargoError` with a readable message?
cards.back: `impl From<ParseIntError> for CargoError` (used by `?`) and `impl fmt::Display for CargoError` (the human message, via `write!` in a `match self`). Usually also `#[derive(Debug)]`.
